author: Anushka Mishra
title: The  Afghanistan Peace Process (2001–2021): Why Negotiations failed to achieve Conflict transformation?
content:
Introduction

 

Amongst the litany of maladies that the mystical land of Afghanistan had to suffer, the persistent crisis of governance and stability surpasses all. The plight of the people is often captured and accurately so by scholars constantly invoking Alexander Pope's line: "fools rush in where angels fear to tread".  The dawn of the twentieth century did not bring a shining ray of light for Afghanistan, which underwent repeated cycles of regime collapse, insurgency, external interference, and political fragmentation. Reformist modernisation under Amanullah Khan, People's Democratic Party of Afghanistan (PDPA) socialism, the mujahideen civil wars, Taliban rule, and post-2001 state-building have all failed to produce durable peace or stability. Each bequeathed its own grievance to the next: reform imposed from above bred rural revolt, ideology invited foreign armies, factional war fractured the polity along ethnic lines, and theocratic rule answered that disorder with repression. By 2001, the conflict inherited was not one war but the sediment of many. The academic terminologies of conflict transformation or conflict resolution have all been invoked to make sense of Afghan politics, but  there is no easy answer to which precisely fits the context.

 

As Lederach and Burgess argue, conflict transformation is a prerequisite to conflict resolution. When applied to Afghanistan, there parties primarily involved in the table of negotiation are from the West and are Afghans, who hold a very negative connotation of each other with respect to values, worldview and geopolitical strategy. Even amongst the Afghanis, there exists a contention between the Taliban and Afghan government officials, where the former perceives the latter as mere American puppets. An atmosphere with such intensity makes it irrevocably impossible to bring all parties to the peace negotiation table, let alone arrive at a common juncture. Here lies the deeper misdiagnosis. Afghanistan was treated as a conflict of interests, solvable through incentives, when in truth the divide was one of values — a pluralist republic against a totalitarian emirate.1 The tools of incentives can bring forth signatures but the deeply embedded values that the signatories carry with them remain at stark conflict still.

 

Although the two sides did not particularly share a common ground, they were not in complete disarray of thoughts either. Both invoked Islam as the fount of legitimacy, both claimed the mantle of Afghan sovereignty against foreign design, and both reached, when it suited them, for the old instruments of consultation such as the jirga (Afghan assembly of  elders. Yet the same vocabulary served opposite ends, for what one read as an Islamic republic, the other read as apostasy dressed in constitutional robes. The tragedy was not that common ground did not exist, but that it was never made the ground on which the parties were asked to stand. Shared cultural resources lay unmobilized while the negotiations busied themselves with troop numbers and timetables, the very definition of a process that touched interests but left values untouched.

 

During protracted conflict, each side views the other with a cascading lens of caricature, the Taliban as nothing but medieval zealotry, Kabul as nothing but American puppetry, and these images become brutal as both sides start to identify themselves with what they are not. Transformation works upon precisely this- not the terms a party will accept, but the picture it carries of its adversary. Conflict transformation, as exhibited by Lederach, assists in reforming the images and reshaping the relationships between each other and their mutual dilemmas, which is the exact intervention that is required in the hinge of Hindu Kush.

 

The Bonn "original sin": a victor's peace (2001)

 

There have been mainly three opportunities presented to the main parties of the Afghan war - the Taliban, the Government of the Islamic Republic of Afghanistan and the United States, between the span of 2001-2021, all of which have been deemed as missed opportunities. A popular internet jest circulated saying, “it took four US presidents, thousands of lives, trillion of dollars, and twenty years to replace the Taliban with the Taliban”. The opportunities of establishing peace were always either fogged out because of some other ‘priorities’ or were rejected on purpose by one or more parties. The Bonn agreement, with the misfortune of happening as the immediate aftermath of 9/11 was imbued with sentiments of retribution and disdain, and thus was doomed from the start. The Bush administration was hardly hesitant at displaying their determination of going to war with the purpose of usurping terrorism from its core, flagging the ultimatum of “you are either with us or against us” to all nations. The Americans were only willing to negotiate with the Taliban with the goal of  persuading them to hand over Osama bin Laden, with CIA station chief in Islamabad, Robert Grenier making active efforts. The Taliban exhibit the ethics of Pashtunwali, the Pashtun code in which melmastia (hospitality) and nanawatai (the obligation to grant sanctuary to one who seeks it) are binding obligations of honour, not preferences to be traded away, which prevented them from handing over a haven-seeker to foreign power. However, the extent of political and cultural motive exuded in this decision is still under debate in the scholarly realm. 

 

The “Bonn process” included building an interim government, followed by drafting a new constitution, eventually resulting in full-fledged democratic elections. Laced with the principles of democracy, one of the major shortcomings of Bonn was the conspicuous absence of Taliban, which UN special representative for Afghanistan Lakhdar Brahimi, referred to as “the original sin”. As time and again pointed out, the Bonn was not laden with the idea of peace but rather was aimed at securing order and stability through parties that were deemed to achieve it, and in the eyes of Americans, that party in question was definitely not the Taliban. Not only was the Taliban not included in the talks, they were active attempts to isolate them. When the US-backed Karzai government seemed to have come to a truce with the Taliban that offered safe passage to Mullah Omar (its founder),the request was blatantly rejected by Rumsfeld [US Secretary of Defense], remarking that “those who harbor terrorists need to be brought to justice”. 2

The two fold isolation attack on Taliban came from US policy, at one hand, which was driven with counterterrorism aggressively chasing al-Qaeda and the Taliban. On the other hand, Northern Alliance leaders were more than elated to savour the perks they received by handing over the Taliban prisoners to the Americans. Thomas Barfield, a scholar of Afghanistan writes, “the time to win the peace is at the end of a war” 3 a principle that vividly went unrecognised by the victors of the Afghan war. The repercussions of it was Afghanistan falling into the rubble of corrupt and predatory power brokers. These individuals were backed by the US, unable to produce good governance while also marginalizing Pashtuns in the process.. The failure of the power transition and the ensued instability was fascinatingly summed up by one Kabul’s intelligence chief, Amrullah Saleh, “Maybe 15% of the people support the government and 5% support the Taliban; everyone else is just stuck in the middle, worried if they pick a side they will be targeted.” 4

 

Statebuilding without peacemaking (2004–2014)

 

In Afghanistan, the war was fought on one end and the peace was settling on another, and both rarely ever spoke or so much as exchanged glances. After the fall of Kabul in 2001, the allied powers were aggressively engrossed in state building and peace became an afterthought. Until 2009, when Barack Obama came to office, the US showed no interest in lending an olive branch of communication directly to a senior Taliban representative. Obama and Hillary Clinton planned to change exactly that by applying a top-down approach and for the first time since 9/11, the graveyard of empires saw some talks that were not hard on military lines. The opening came from both sides at once, an American admission that the war could not be won by arms alone, and a Taliban leadership pressed by Mullah Omar's failing health and the attrition of the surge. 5 The precondition put down by Hilary Clinton - lay down weapons, reject al-Qaeda and respect the 2004 constitution - for talks with Taliban eventually became the outcome. However, this channel of communication also became a missed opportunity. There were debates within the US and NATO forces, where one commander, McChrystal, propagated for soft diplomacy to win “hearts and minds” of Afghans, whereas General Petraeus was adamant on bending Taliban to their knees through increased military intervention. 

In the eyes of many Afghans, the Taliban’s attacks established the members as valiant fighters against a foreign occupier and its puppet, the Kabul government. The series of bombings made the public lose faith in the republican government and also in the United States, a loss that never recovered again. Moreover, under the new government, Afghanistan became a rentier state with a chunk of its capital flowing from the drug economy and foreign aid. The problem with rentier states(a state funded by external rents rather than its citizens' tax), is that their rulers tend to be unlikely to develop effective tax systems, accountability for spending patterns, or capable autonomous bureaucracies, or to invest in local productive enterprises. On the political front, domestic institutions lose accountability as it is more tilted towards the donors. All of this considered, the fall of Najibulla, who fell to rubbles in 1975 when Soviet funds dried up, was still afresh in the minds of Afghans. A sum of USD 28.5 billion of aid requirements were estimated to promote post-war development in Afghanistan under the seven-year plan titled ‘Saving Afghanistan's Future’. Ashraf Ghani, the Finance Minister back then, warned that Afghanistan is most likely to become a narco-mafia state if things continued in this order.

 

What is striking is how little the Taliban's script changed over the following decade. In talks, the refrain was always the same: the fault lay with the United States. Washington, they argued, had invaded and toppled a legitimate Islamic Emirate. The 2004 constitution counted for nothing, written as it was under the threat of American bombers. From this it followed, in their telling, that there was only one party worth negotiating, the United States itself. The government in Kabul they dismissed as a puppet, not worth the trouble of a conversation. This was a convenient read. The Republic had its failings, but it also had elections, a press, and a generation of women in classrooms, and calling it a puppet was less conviction than tactic, a way of insisting that only Washington was worth talking to. A deeper misconception that drove US leaders was their relentless effort at bleeding down Taliban leaders through America’s military prowess, hoping the latter would eventually fall, giving the US an upper hand at the negotiation table. This misreading could be beautifully captured in one of the Pashtun once quoted by a Taliban commander, “You have the watches, but we have the time.”  The problem here lied in the warped understanding of what the policymakers exactly wanted and what they were actually achieving. Peace which became a footnote was decimated to something even lower. It was discarded entirely, in the process of maintaining the military might to keep the Taliban at bay, while the populace kept losing hope in the new US- backed regime.

 

The missing "ripe moment": why the timing never aligned

 

In the midst of the Nagorno-Karabakh conflict in 1992, Iran's deputy foreign minister observed that the situation "is not ripe for such moves for mediation", a diagnosis that could, with little alteration, have been pronounced over Afghanistan across two decades of missed openings.6  The Taliban commander’s comment on time becomes quite crucial as when we deliberate over negotiations and conflict resolution, the star of the show is “correct timing”. An old saying of, “You get nothing before your time, nor more than your destiny” accurately fits the description. The negotiation rarely ever takes place because the parties involved are ardently unwilling to put down their arms, sit and talk. William Zartan theorizes the “riping theory”, where negotiations happen when the timing is ripe. The concept of ripe timing centers on the parties’ perception of a Mutually Hurting Stalemate (MHS), optimally associated with an impending, past or recently avoided catastrophe.7 The concept is based on the notion that when the parties find themselves locked in a conflict from which they cannot escalate to victory and this deadlock is painful to both, they seek an alternative policy or Way Out.8

Afghanistan was presented with three such opportunities, all of which were missed. In the first instance neither of the two winning alliances deemed it necessary to include the sole defeater in the negotiation talks, in the second instance it was the overindulgent foreign intervention and domestic corruption which overlooked every opportunity of peacebuilding and the third instance witnessed what everyone in the second phase, the US troops withdrew and Kabul once again fell into the hands of Taliban. This is where the “watches and time” analogy is crucial. The reason why Taliban was able to outlast the clock was because of the safe refuge they were receiving in Pakistan. Despite giving aid to them from a distance, even Pakistan did not bring up the point of bringing the Taliban to the negotiation table during the Bonn process, with the sword of ‘with us or against us’ in the WoT statements by Bush.

 

Doha and the sequencing error: negotiating withdrawal, not peace (2018–2020)

 

The year 2018 arrived bearing what looked like the long-awaited turn towards peace. President Trump, restless to end the "forever war", appointed Zalmay Khalilzad as special representative, and for the first time the United States engaged directly with the Taliban.9 Yet, what was dressed in the vestments of a peace process was, at its marrow, far narrower. As William Maley has argued, the agreement made more sense as an exit agreement than a peace agreement, carrying nothing on democracy, nothing on minorities, nothing on the position of women, and nothing on the Pakistani sanctuaries that were the lifeblood of Taliban operations. 10 Peace was not so much negotiated as quietly written out.

The gravest wound lay in the sequencing. Washington abandoned its own principle, that nothing is agreed until everything is agreed,  and struck a bilateral deal with the Taliban first, leaving the Afghan government to negotiate its fate afterwards.11  By the time the Republic was ushered to the table, the Americans had already surrendered everything the Taliban craved, and above all, a fixed timetable for withdrawal. 12 Excluded from both the making of the agreement and the agreement itself, and not even shown its full text, Ghani felt betrayed.13 The wiser course was the one Washington had itself begun with, that nothing be agreed until everything was agreed, holding the withdrawal timetable in reserve until the Taliban had conceded a ceasefire and genuine talks with Kabul. Ghani's presence at the table would have changed the arithmetic considerably. The prisoners were his to trade, the agreement would have been his to own rather than disown, and the Taliban could not have dismissed the intra-Afghan talks as subordinate to a bargain the Republic had played no part in striking. Whether he would have used that seat well is another matter, for he misread American intentions badly and commanded little unity even among his own. Yet exclusion guaranteed the outcome when inclusion merely risked it, and here Bonn returned in mirror image, the vanquished shut out in 2001, the government shut out in 2020.

Brooking's verdict is unsparing: these were not peace negotiations, but negotiations over the safe withdrawal of US forces.14 Herein lies the thread binding this failure to every failure before it. The process reached only for the arithmetic of exit, troops, timetables, prisoners, and never touched the relational or the structural, neither approaching the reshaping of relationships that transformation demands. It was a settlement of departure masquerading as a settlement of the war.

Why a settlement was never a transformation (synthesis)

 

Were the negotiations and mediation in Afghanistan ever doomed to fail, or a different approach and technique would have done the trick of producing a better outcome? The question looms over the angle of looking at the conflict, but it is the vantage point that is problematic here. For the two decades what unravelled in the land of Afghanistan under the garb of peace - was state building, foreign chokehold, chasm of understanding between involved parties, politics of discourse and image building and a lack of meaningful governance. So, what has been deemed as the failure of the peace process, from Bonn to Doha, a major blot has been in understanding the goals of stakeholders. The tragedy of Afghanistan was not that its peace was mishandled, but that a peace, in the fuller sense the word demands, was never genuinely attempted.

While the flag of peace tried to unfurl, the ghost of today during Bonn sidelines the vanquished and sketched victor’s peace as final settlement, the bridge period of reconstruction saw openings for reconciliation which was always forced at the backseat in the name of addressing other pressing concerns, and eventually the Doha marked the exiting of troops as another feather in the barret. Each attempt bargained over biased interests and timelines, none looked into the conflict of values, reshaping of images and overall reconciliation of clash of thought to establish a lasting peace in the valley.

Herein lies the true tragedy of Afghanistan. Where peace was not ousted or somersaulted, it was unfortunately never attempted. The parties involved were not particularly against peace. They also pulled the chair on the negotiation table vested with their own interest, which was often achieved without the prevalence of peace. The Taliban's motive was victory and the US interests lied in exit, none of which significantly required peace to be the precedent of those events. While one party kept pooling military might to the country, another reveled in the luxury of dono’s charity, while the third honed the present animosity for both the former parties. In between that, peace found no refuge. A war whose roots were left untouched could yield what the outcome did: the return, two decades on, of the very order the intervention had set out to undo.

 

Conclusion

 

The tale of Afghanistan is one of great power politics and of an Oriental understanding (a western-perception of the East, term coined by Edward Said). It remained a mere purview of dealing with the east, where everybody was far too fixated over ending the war which was always misread as establishment of peace, when both are two very different approaches to negotiation.  A 2007 American release, Charlie Wilson’s war, evokes the frustration of one of the US Congressman at the closing who remarks that the US "changed the world" in Afghanistan and then abandoned it, and that this neglect of the endgame is what mattered. If there is a lesson to be drawn for the wicked problems that will follow elsewhere, it is a plain one: that a peace which addresses only the interests of those who fight, while leaving untouched the values and relationships that set them fighting, is no peace at all, but merely an interval between wars.
